title: Diode small-signal model and diffusion capacitance

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
For small signals around a DC operating point, the exponential diode looks like a straight line: a **small-signal conductance** \(g_d\), the slope of the I–V curve. Because the slope of an exponential is proportional to its value, \(g_d\) is simply the bias current divided by the thermal voltage.

A forward-biased diode also stores injected minority charge in its neutral regions. That charge rises with current, giving a **diffusion capacitance** \(C_d\) that sits in parallel with the junction capacitance \(C_j\). In forward bias \(C_d\) usually dominates. The small-signal model is valid only for swings well under \(kT/q\).

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ g_d = \frac{dI_D}{dV_D} = \frac{qI_D}{kT}, \qquad r_d = \frac{1}{g_d} = \frac{kT/q}{I_D} \]
\[ C_d = g_d\,\tau_T \]
where \(\tau_T\) is the transit time (short base, \(\tau_T = W^2/2D\)) or the lifetime (long base).
Small-signal model: \(g_d \parallel C_d \parallel C_j\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
A diode is biased at \(I_D = 0.26\ \mathrm{mA}\) with a transit time of 1 ns.
\[ g_d = \frac{0.26\ \mathrm{mA}}{26\ \mathrm{mV}} = 10\ \mathrm{mS}, \qquad r_d = 100\ \Omega \]
\[ C_d = 10^{-2}\times10^{-9} = 10\ \mathrm{pF} \]
The corner where \(g_d\) and \(C_d\) are equal is \(g_d/C_d = 10^{9}\ \mathrm{rad/s}\), set by the transit time alone.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Using \(V_D/I_D\) (large-signal ratio) as the small-signal resistance.
- Forgetting \(C_d\) grows with current while \(C_j\) is nearly fixed.
- Applying the model to swings comparable to 26 mV.
- Mixing \(g_d\) and \(r_d\) units (S versus Ω).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: The same small-signal thinking (slope of a large-signal law at the bias point) is how transistor models are built, with transconductance taking the place of \(g_d\).
